title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1; preregistration SHA-256 archived) and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation of operator intent into device configuration promises faster NetOps workflows but creates operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Recent literature and system proposals recommend generate→verify→repair designs that pair probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators or simulators as floor‑safety nets. However, rigorous preregistered, paired A/B experiments that quantify the practical benefit of such guarded pipelines under reproducible sampling semantics remain scarce. This paper presents a narrowly scoped preregistered paired experiment that tests whether a minimal guarded pipeline—a single shared LLM candidate per task, a frozen deterministic validator, and at most one automated repair attempt—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate versus the same LLM’s plain single‑shot output. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic task seeding and full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) confirmatory results showing a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) and one corrected discordance by the guarded pipeline; (3) an artifact‑grounded post‑hoc sensitivity analysis demonstrating why the preregistered effect size target could not be evaluated under the observed data; and (4) practical methodological recommendations—grounded in the archived preregistration and execution manifest—for designing future confirmatory NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and system papers document that LLMs can synthesize configuration templates and translate intent into device commands in controlled settings, while also cataloguing failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety. Work in adjacent domains (medical QA, code generation) shows that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and bounded repair loops reduce factual errors, motivating similar architectures for NetOps. Architectures combining LLM agents with deterministic validators and human approval are recurring recommendations in recent agentic NetOps proposals. Nevertheless, the literature lacks reproducible, preregistered paired A/B experiments that (a) use deterministically generated task banks, (b) freeze validators and repair budgets, and (c) report complete execution accounting with archived artifacts. Our study situates itself at that gap by providing a preregistered paired test with archived model calls, validator traces, and analysis artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the confirmatory design (study id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and froze the analysis plan prior to execution. Two confirmatory hypotheses were registered: H1— the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2—one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a planning assumption of baseline pass rate = 0.40 to compute sample size and power; that literal planning assumption and the preregistration artifact are archived (preregistration SHA-256: 4a00a81629acfd3f1fb5d0a04cea795a52261270e7dc63bf7d3cb63cc11afda0) and are reported here to make the preregistered power rationale transparent.

Design, sampling, and pairing semantics: The experiment used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated task seeds. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate was shared between arms (the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics): baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same candidate validated and, if invalid, subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). Planned episodes = 600; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate pairing was preregistered and reduces within‑pair variability but also reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available for McNemar inference relative to independent draws per arm; this design choice was intentional and specified before execution.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, canonicalizes configurations to a normalized AST, and produces a binary pass/fail score with violation codes that drive repair attempts. The scoring rule is full intent‑constraint validation: outputs are scored as successes only when the validator confirms required command sequences and dependency constraints. Provider/model failures were handled per the preregistered missingness plan (one retry allowed; primary analysis treatment 'complete_pair_primary' drops pairs only if both calls fail).

Task bank and canonicalization: Tasks were synthetically generated from a frozen deterministic task generator producing intent→expected configuration pairs with explicit required sequences and workflow policies. Each task payload included initial and expected final states, allowed touched fields, and dependency constraints; the validator’s canonicalizer normalized commands to an AST to enable deterministic equality and constraint checking. Contamination detection and deterministic replacement rules for near‑duplicates were preregistered and executed during the run; task inclusion/exclusion decisions and counts are enumerated in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301; only a single repair‑stage model call was invoked under the preregistered repair budget. There were no provider or infrastructure failures under the retry policy; the execution manifest confirms full pair accounting and reconciliation.

Primary outcomes (artifact‑derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency table (archived): n11 = 299, n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0, n00 = 0. These counts were directly computed from the archived per‑task scoring output and form the input to confirmatory inference.

Statistical inference and sensitivity: Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for this absolute difference (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01], as recorded in the analysis outputs. The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); the exact Clopper–Pearson 95% interval for 1/1 is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting extreme uncertainty from a single observed repair event.

Why the preregistered H1 could not be confirmed: The preregistration used a planning assumption of baseline pass rate = 0.40 and computed that N=300 paired tasks would provide >80% power to detect an absolute difference ≥0.20 (roughly baseline 0.40 → guarded 0.70). The observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and leaves effectively zero statistical headroom: with only one discordant pair (n10 + n01 = 1) the maximal resolvable absolute paired difference equals 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 and the exact McNemar test cannot reject the null. The archived bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) confirms that plausible absolute improvement under the observed data is orders of magnitude smaller than the preregistered target. This post‑hoc sensitivity bound is derived directly from the archived contingency counts and bootstrap resampling recorded in the analysis artifact bundle.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline successfully corrected the single observed invalid baseline output in this run, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, because the baseline pass rate was far higher than the preregistered planning assumption, this run does not provide confirmatory evidence for the preregistered large relative reduction target (≥50%). The artifact record supports only the narrower operational claim that, in this task bank and with this model/validator pair, the guarded pipeline achieved a final validated success rate of 100% while the baseline was 99.667%.

Design lessons grounded in artifacts: (1) Difficulty calibration: preregistered power calculations hinged on an assumed baseline pass rate (0.40). If a task bank yields a near‑ceiling baseline, even large relative improvements are untestable. We therefore recommend preregistering target counts of initial failures (i.e., expected number of informative discordant pairs) or calibrating task‑generation parameters so that the planned N yields sufficient discordant‑pair expectation for the target effect. (2) Pairing semantics and repair budgets: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate choice reduces variance but also reduces discordance opportunity; experiment designers should explicitly account for this tradeoff when computing power for paired tests. (3) Repair estimands: when baseline pass rates are uncertain, treat repair success as a conditional estimand (repair efficacy conditional on initial failure) and power the study to accrue enough initial failures to estimate that conditional rate precisely.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate pairing and deterministic seed list were preregistered and executed as specified; they reduce confounding but limit discordance. Construct validity: validation was static—based on canonicalized AST checks and workflow constraints—so runtime packet‑level or control‑plane effects were not measured. External validity: the synthetic task bank, limited vendor‑template space, a single model (gpt-5-mini), and a single validator implementation restrict generality. Conclusion validity: inference about large effect sizes is precluded by the near‑ceiling baseline and the resulting paucity of discordant pairs; the archived contingency counts quantify this limit.

Concrete sample‑sizing guidance from the archived preregistration: using the preregistered planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40, N=300 paired tasks was computed to provide >80% power to detect absolute differences ≥0.20 at α=0.05 under conservative discordant assumptions. That numerical example illustrates how preregistered baseline assumptions map into detectable absolute differences; experimenters should either calibrate task difficulty to obtain the assumed baseline or adjust N (or the effect target) accordingly.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment with N=300 deterministically seeded tasks, a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs produced guarded = 300/300 valid configurations and baseline = 299/300 valid configurations. The single automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction hypothesis because the observed baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should preregister target counts of initial failures (not only overall N), choose pairing semantics consistent with inferential goals, and—when operational claims require runtime assurances—incorporate emulation/simulation that exercises packet‑ or control‑plane semantics rather than relying solely on static deterministic validators. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic canonicalized configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; packet‑level reachability, performance, and control‑plane side effects were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
